headline: zerobrew offers 100x faster Homebrew alternative for macOS and Linux
summary: zerobrew uses a uv-style architecture to significantly speed up package installations, leveraging Homebrew's existing bottle build farm for macOS and Linux users. It's currently experimental but promises massive performance gains.
details: zerobrew is an experimental alternative to Homebrew for macOS and Linux, promising up to 100x faster package installations. It achieves this by adopting a uv-style architecture, optimizing the post-download installation process.

Unlike Homebrew, which uses Ruby to evaluate formulae and re-signs binaries one at a time, zerobrew performs relocation in-process. It links from a content-addressed store, reducing overhead after the initial download.

The project emphasizes that it relies entirely on Homebrew's bottle build farm for packages. zerobrew does not compile anything or maintain formulae; its speed comes solely from its optimized installation method.
Benchmarks conducted on macOS with a MacBook Pro (M3 Pro) showed significant speed improvements. The project's CI ensures zerobrew remains at least 1.5x faster cold and 3x faster warm than Homebrew.
Developers are advised to run zerobrew alongside Homebrew rather than as a full replacement due to its experimental nature. Users should be fully aware of the implications before purging Homebrew.
caption:

headline_marked: LLM [[ports TypeScript compiler to Rust]] for $24k, 1.6x faster than Go version
headline: LLM ports TypeScript compiler to Rust for $24k, 1.6x faster than Go version
summary: An LLM successfully ported the TypeScript compiler to Rust for just $24,047, achieving 100% compatibility and a 1.6x speedup over the original Go version. This demonstrates significant AI-driven code generation capabilities.
details: An experimental project successfully used an LLM to port the TypeScript compiler, checker, and language server to Rust. This ambitious undertaking resulted in a functional `tsc-rs` that boasts 100% compatibility across tested real-world projects.

Initial attempts with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT 6 Astra models were costly, consuming over $400,000 in tokens and generating 1.3 million lines of Rust code. Despite the high expense, these models only reached about 84% compatibility after months of iterative development.

Switching to Claude Opus 5.5 proved far more efficient. It started from scratch and produced a working v0 in 10 hours, achieving higher compatibility much faster. The total API token spend for Opus 5.5 was approximately $24,047 over two weeks.

`tsc-rs` is a direct port of Microsoft's native TypeScript compiler, which was originally written in Go. It maintains the same algorithms, behavior, command line interface (`tsc`), language server, and API as the upstream project.

The `tsc-rs` npm package is designed to avoid conflicts with the existing `typescript` package. Standalone archives are also available for Linux x64 and macOS arm64 platforms, with Windows and Linux arm64 support planned.

Performance benchmarks show `tsc-rs` is notably faster than the Go-based `tsc 7`, achieving a 1.61x speedup on average across various open-source applications. While `bun check` is generally faster, `tsc-rs` offers built-in Effect language service diagnostics.

The integrated Effect language service diagnostics (codes 377xxx) mean that Effect projects do not require a second compiler pass. These diagnostics are derived from the same check as TypeScript diagnostics and are visible in the language server, activating only when the relevant plugin is configured.
